title: Hammer
prompt: a hammer beside a nail in a wood block on a table with three buttons: “Raise” lifts the hammer about a model wrist pivot; “Strike” swings the head into the nail; “Reset” replaces the nail; see-through reveals the wrist fulcrum, hand effort and head travel of the third-class lever
chapter: Part 1: The Mechanics of Movement / Levers
blurb: A teaching hand swings a hammer about the wrist to drive a nail, showing the greater travel of the head.

identity.note: Levers / Third-class levers / Hammer, page 23. Wrist fulcrum and hand effort make the head travel farther and faster to drive a nail against wood resistance.
identity.classificationNote: A named machine or diagram inside Levers is not a separate main chapter. The parking-meter heading is historical.

adaptationDecision.reason: Distinct from claw-hammer, now titled Nail extractor. Extraction has a first-class pivot against wood; striking has a wrist fulcrum. Do not combine both actions in either brief.

prompt.note: Faithful labelled adaptation. A model wrist and hand make the book's analogy explicit. Raise, Strike and Reset stage the lesson. Distinguish impact from static leverage. Do not claim third-class leverage multiplies force or use claw contact as the striking pivot.
prompt.apparatusRelation: Bench or scale teaching adaptation of a named book example. Controls, fixtures and test specimens stage the lesson and are not claimed as the book apparatus.

truthNotes: A third-class lever increases head speed and travel, not static force. Impact drives the nail.
Partial model hand and forearm make the wrist fulcrum explicit. The transverse wrist marker is a diagram overlay, not a pin through a human wrist.
Table, wood block, staged motion and nail replacement are teaching adaptations. Reset is specimen replacement, not nail extraction or self-repair.
One-piece steel hammer with a molded grip is a representative construction. The inactive claw has no pivot contact or extraction action.

Travel ratio uses radii of 60 and 14 model units, rounded to 4.3. One model unit represents 5 mm; timing is slowed. Nail penetration follows the contact face height in a prescribed illustrative motion; no impact force, energy or material-response prediction.
1988 remains inaccessible and unverified; no edition-union claim.
